title: Sunway D'Hill: forest views with city convenience.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #459 | SUNWAY D'HILL, KOTA DAMANSARA
excerpt: A completed mixed development backing onto a forest reserve, where the arrival sequence, the car park and the landscape deck all show a developer refining the same playbook.
takeaways: Separating the commercial entrance at the front from the residential entrance at the back is the single decision Sean rates most highly here.
The facilities deck is the densest landscape treatment he has reviewed, designed across sunken and elevated levels to slow residents down.
Buying a completed project removes the three-to-four year wait, but five or six new launches are already coming up one street away.

sections.heading: Two roads, and how the address changed
paragraphs: Sean orients himself before looking at the building. Persiaran Mahogani is the long inner road serving the residential side; Persiaran Surian, one street over, is the commercial spine connecting to the hospital, colleges and malls. D'Hill sits on the quiet one, backing onto a forest reserve his episode notes put at around 800 acres.

The history matters to his argument. This pocket was where locals built large private homes precisely because it was serene and away from the action. Then the action arrived: the MRT began running and the DASH highway completed, and what used to be reached by an old back road became one of the more sought-after addresses in the area.

He adds a forward-looking note. A brand new township is being developed a single street away, which will keep bringing development to this address for years — though he is clear that a master plan of that size takes fifteen to twenty years to mature.

sections.heading: Keeping shoppers and residents apart
paragraphs: This is a mixed development, and the first thing Sean praises is the separation of access. The retail level has its own entrance and boom gate at the front; residents drive around to a separate entrance at the back. Nobody heading home has to queue behind somebody going to the shops.

The retail row was already filling up at handover — a supermarket, a pharmacy, a clinic, an optical shop and a hardware chain among roughly 29 units. The detail he singles out is ownership: the developer has retained all of the retail rather than selling it off, so the tenant mix stays under one hand instead of drifting toward whoever pays the highest rent.
Behind the shops runs a dedicated service lane for refuse and stock deliveries, with the service pipes routed along it. Lorries load out of sight, and the front of the scheme stays tidy.

sections.heading: An arrival sequence built like an office lobby
paragraphs: The residential drop-off sits enclosed within the car park structure, which makes it weatherproof and private — a treatment Sean has now seen across several of this developer's recent projects and clearly rates. Heavy rain does not reach anyone getting out of a car.

The columns are structural but dressed: landscaped islands, timber cladding and pavers soften what would otherwise read as a concrete undercroft. He compares the effect to the drop-off of a convention centre or a grade-A office rather than a condominium.

It is also naturally ventilated throughout, with water features used sparingly to break up the column lines. No air conditioning in the common areas means a lighter maintenance burden, and each of the two towers gets its own private lobby beyond the shared arrival point.

sections.heading: Why the car park is worth talking about
paragraphs: Six levels of parking are served by two speed ramps — one from ground to level two, a second running straight from level two to level six. Sean's point is about lived experience: even parking on the top deck, the drive up is quick, because you are not spiralling through every intermediate floor.

The construction is a flat slab system with cemented floors, epoxy-painted pedestrian lanes and bays about 2.55 m wide. Because the land falls away, daylight reaches into the structure and the edge nearest the drop-off is left half open, so the space cross-ventilates instead of feeling closed in.

He points out a cheap detail he considers genuinely clever: guard rails around the speed ramp. They serve almost no safety function, since nobody walks there — but they make the ramp instantly readable from a distance, so drivers spot the turn and take it without hunting.

sections.heading: The most worked landscape deck he has reviewed
paragraphs: The facilities take Sean more than half an hour to walk, and he calls the landscape treatment the densest he has covered. The lap pool carries an infinity edge that frames the forest when you are in the water; the pool surround is pebble wash for grip, with a shaded wading pool and seating where parents can actually sit.

The design intent he identifies is deceleration. Paths sway left and right rather than running straight, and the deck moves between sunken and elevated levels so the same landscape is experienced from several heights. An elevated walkway threads through the planting to a herb garden, a steel pavilion and a webbed hammock structure set among the foliage.

The rest is unusually complete: a barbecue deck with a sunken lounge, a glass-clad cantilevered gym looking into the forest, a multi-sports hall with a nine-metre ceiling, a sunken basketball court positioned so the ball stays in, and a furnished co-working space. Play areas are split by age group over rubber matting, and Sean notes the invisible netting added where children might climb.

sections.heading: Corridors, and the details nobody photographs
paragraphs: Two towers hold roughly 976 units, arranged thirteen to a floor along a double-loaded corridor with a central void. The lift lobby runs about 2.95 m wide under a 2.7 m ceiling; the corridor itself is around 1.75 m wide.

The detail Sean keeps returning to across this developer's work is the zero transition — no step anywhere from the ground floor drop-off through to the bedroom. He points out how much that matters with a stroller or a wheelchair, and the entrance foyer at 1.6 m is wide enough for a real shoe cabinet.

He also approves of the fire partition doors held open on magnetic locks that release with the alarm, so nobody wrestles a heavy door daily; and the refuse room, which is naturally ventilated behind two sets of doors so smell never reaches the lift lobby. The parapet to the void is 1.2 m, spray painted, with drainage and covered windows where rain used to blow into the corridor.

sections.heading: Inside the four-bedroom unit
paragraphs: The unit filmed is a Type D of about 1,238 sq ft with four bedrooms and three bathrooms — though Sean is careful to flag that this one is a show unit, so the fittings are not what a buyer receives bare. Entry leads past a dry kitchen to a dining area and a living space of roughly 3.45 m wall to wall under a 2.8 m ceiling, ending in a balcony that frames the forest.

He rates the separate wet kitchen highly. A glass sliding door shuts it off from the dry kitchen, so heavy cooking does not reach the furniture outside, with the yard and compressor space beyond it. The balcony runs about 3.2 m by 1.4 m, fully tiled, with slight tinting to cut heat and glare and no overlooking from the adjacent block.

The two children's bedrooms are near-identical in size and share the same outlook, which he notes with amusement settles any argument between siblings. His one reservation is the junior suite beside the dining area — the only room exposed to the shared living space, which makes it awkward when guests are over unless it becomes a study or home office.

sections.heading: Noise, crowding and what completion is worth
paragraphs: His concerns start with the micro-site. Persiaran Mahogani is wide and straight, and against such quiet surroundings every acceleration on a four-lane road carries. The immediate neighbourhood also mixes social housing and older apartments with the large private homes — the original character of a location that only recently became desirable.

The retail is a double-edged benefit. As the nearest grocer for the area it will draw crowds, and he expects congestion once more food and beverage operators move in; traffic here is still managed only by traffic lights. That the developer owns and manages the whole commercial component, with the service lane keeping lorries out of sight, is what keeps him comfortable with it.

The last concern is competition: five or six new projects are already rising in the township across the street, which means more homework for buyers. But he turns that into D'Hill's strongest practical argument — it is finished. You can pick your block, orientation and unit, inspect the actual build quality, and move in now rather than waiting three or four years. Pricing discussed in the episode worked out around RM700 per square foot, with the four-bedroom unit filmed at about RM850,000; those figures reflect the recording date and one specific unit.

pros: The commercial entrance sits at the front and the residential entrance at the back, so residents never share a queue with shoppers, and the enclosed drop-off within the car park structure stays weatherproof and private.

The facilities deck is the densest landscape treatment he has reviewed — circulation that deliberately slows you down, sunken and elevated levels, and structural elements tidy enough to keep the car park below efficient.

The site strikes a genuine balance between urbanism and nature: schools, hospital, MRT, university and the DASH highway are all close by one road, while every unit is turned to face the forest reserve.
cons: Persiaran Mahogani is too wide and too straight, so traffic noise from a four-lane road carries into an otherwise quiet setting, and the immediate surroundings still mix social housing and older apartments.
The retail component will draw the whole neighbourhood as the nearest grocer, and with traffic controlled only by lights he expects congestion once more operators open.
Five or six new projects are already coming up in the township one street away, which means far more comparison work for buyers.

closing: Sunway D'Hill reads as a developer refining a playbook it has used before — the drop-off, the speed ramps, the zero transition — and applying it to a site whose forest backdrop does the rest. Its clearest advantage over everything rising across the street is simply that you can move in and see exactly what you bought.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full public English captions and his published YouTube episode notes. Measurements, unit size and pricing are as stated in the video and reflect the recording date; the unit filmed was a show unit. The 3 on 3 section paraphrases the three things Sean says he likes and the three he has concerns about, presented near the end of the episode.
